title: Trapping Rain Water
description: Brute force to optimized: rescanning both directions versus precomputed max arrays versus two pointers.

blocks.text: Given an array height representing an elevation map where each value is the height of a bar of width 1, compute how much water can be trapped between the bars after it rains.

blocks.title: Analogy: Water Pooling Between City Skyscrapers
blocks.text: Picture a row of buildings of different heights. After a rainstorm, water collects in the gaps between taller buildings, and how much water sits at any one spot depends on the shorter of the two tallest buildings visible to its left and to its right, since water can never rise higher than its lowest surrounding wall.

blocks.caption: Water at each position is bounded by the shorter of the tallest walls on either side

blocks.text: With strictly increasing heights, there is no wall on the right side tall enough to hold any water in, so no water is trapped anywhere, giving 0.
It helps to ask exactly which information each position genuinely needs, and whether it has to be recomputed every time.

blocks.title: How Should We Think?
blocks.text:
Observation 1: Product of Array Except Self already showed that per-position rescanning can be replaced by precomputing a left array and a right array once each, then combining them in a single pass, the same idea applies here directly to running maximums instead of products.

Observation 2: That still costs O(n) extra space for two full arrays. Three Sum already showed two pointers converging from both ends can replace scanning an entire array, so it is worth asking whether an analogous trick applies here.

Observation 3: It does, but the invariant is subtler than a simple sum comparison: whichever side currently has the smaller running max already has its true water level fully determined, because the wall on the taller side can never be the limiting factor for that position, no matter what lies further along that taller side.

Observation 4: Tracing height equal to [4, 2, 0, 3, 2, 5] confirms it, processing the smaller side first at every step and moving that pointer inward converges on the same total, 9, that the two full precomputed arrays produce, without ever building them.

Proving that the smaller running max always identifies a position whose water level is already fully known is what allows two pointers to replace two full precomputed arrays with just two running integers.

For every position, scan leftward to find the tallest wall on that side and scan rightward to find the tallest wall on that side, then the water trapped there is the shorter of those two walls minus the height at that position, if positive.

items: For every position i, scan everything to its left to find the tallest bar there.
Scan everything to its right to find the tallest bar there.
Water at position i is the minimum of those two walls minus height[i], if that value is positive.
Sum the water trapped across every position.

codes.python:
def trap(height):
    n = len(height)
    total = 0
    for i in range(n):
        left_max = max(height[:i + 1])                          # tallest wall to the left, including here
        right_max = max(height[i:])                               # tallest wall to the right, including here
        total += min(left_max, right_max) - height[i]
    return total


if __name__ == "__main__":
    height = [4, 2, 0, 3, 2, 5]
    print(trap(height))

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Every position independently rescans the array in both directions, so no information about walls is shared or reused between neighboring positions.
The water at a position is exactly the shorter surrounding wall minus its own height, which is naturally non negative whenever a genuine wall exists on both sides.
This directly matches the physical picture of trapped water, but at the cost of scanning most of the array twice for every single position.

blocks.text: The trapped water at each position is correctly bounded by the shorter of the two tallest surrounding walls, so summing this across every position gives the right total.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n squared), rescanning left and right from every single position.
Space: O(1), no extra array is used.
Limitation: the left and right maximums are recomputed by rescanning the array for every position, when they could instead be precomputed once and reused for every lookup.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why the brute force works but is wasteful: it rescans nearly the entire array from every single position, even though the tallest wall to the left of position i and the tallest wall to the left of position i plus 1 differ by at most one comparison.

What precomputed left and right max arrays fix directly: build leftMax in one forward pass and rightMax in one backward pass, so every position's two walls become simple array lookups instead of rescans.

Can the two full arrays themselves be avoided: yes, since only the smaller of a position's two running maxes ever actually determines its water level, the larger side's exact value never needs to be looked up at all.

The core idea: precompute both arrays first to establish correctness and intuition, then recognize that two pointers with two running maxes, always processing the smaller side, achieve the same result without ever materializing either array.

Precompute a left max array in one forward pass, where leftMax[i] holds the tallest wall from the start up through position i, and a right max array in one backward pass, where rightMax[i] holds the tallest wall from position i through the end. Then a single pass combines them: water at position i is the minimum of leftMax[i] and rightMax[i], minus height[i].
Precompute left max and right max arrays, then sum the trapped water in one pass.

blocks.text: This works because leftMax[i] and rightMax[i] correctly capture the tallest wall visible to each side of position i, so the shorter of the two, minus the height already occupying that position, is exactly the depth of water physically able to sit there before overflowing toward the shorter wall.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), three linear passes.
Space: O(n), for the two precomputed arrays.
10. Further Optimization: Two Pointers, No Extra Arrays

Two pointers, one starting at each end of the array, can replace both precomputed arrays entirely. At each step, move the pointer on the side with the smaller running max inward: whichever side has the smaller max is the side whose water level is already fully determined, since the true bounding wall for that position can only be that smaller max or something even smaller further along, never something from the taller side. This lets the water at each position be computed immediately as the pointers cross the array, with no arrays needed at all.

blocks.caption: Further optimization: two pointers, moving the side with the smaller max inward

codes.python:
def trap(height):
    left, right = 0, len(height) - 1
    left_max, right_max = 0, 0
    total = 0
    while left < right:
        if height[left] < height[right]:
            left_max = max(left_max, height[left])
            total += left_max - height[left]                        # water level here is fully determined
            left += 1
        else:
            right_max = max(right_max, height[right])
            total += right_max - height[right]                       # water level here is fully determined
            right -= 1
    return total


if __name__ == "__main__":
    height = [4, 2, 0, 3, 2, 5]
    print(trap(height))

items: Comparing height[left] to height[right] decides which side currently has the smaller running max, since the running max on that side can never exceed the bar it is being compared against.

Processing the smaller side first is safe because its true bounding wall can only be its own running max or something even smaller found later, the taller opposite side can never become the limiting wall for it.
Each processed position immediately adds its water contribution to the running total, so the final total is complete the moment the two pointers meet.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), a single pass with the two pointers meeting in the middle.
Space: O(1), only the two pointers and two running maxes are kept.

blocks.text: The two pointer trick relies on a subtle but important invariant: whichever side currently has the smaller running max is guaranteed to have its true water level already known, because the opposite wall, being taller, could never be the limiting factor for that position.

items: Moving the pointer on the taller side instead of the shorter side, which breaks the invariant the two pointer approach depends on.
Forgetting that water trapped at a position can be 0 or negative before clamping, when the position itself is taller than one of its surrounding walls.

blocks.text: Explain the two pointer invariant carefully in words before coding it. It is the one detail that turns this from a memorized trick into a reasoned solution.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text:
If the interviewer says "can you do this without extra arrays", think: two pointers, always processing whichever side currently has the smaller running max.
If the interviewer says "why is it safe to process the smaller side", think: the opposite, taller wall can never become the limiting factor for that position, no matter what comes later on that side.
If the interviewer says "what if the heights were given as a 2D elevation map", think: this becomes the harder Trapping Rain Water II variant, usually solved with a priority queue instead of two pointers.

items: Why is it always safe to process the side with the smaller running max first?
How would you adapt this approach to a 2D elevation map instead of a 1D array?
How would you return the positions where water is trapped, not just the total volume?
What would change if the bars had different widths instead of all being width 1?
How would you compute the total volume incrementally if the array were updated one element at a time?
Product of Array Except Self, whose precomputed left and right passes are the direct ancestor of the left max and right max arrays used here.
Three Sum, whose two pointers converging from both ends toward the middle is the same overall shape, adapted here with a nontrivial invariant about which side to advance.

Any problem asking for a value at each position that depends on the extremes to its left and right, where precomputing both directions, and later replacing them with two pointers, is the standard approach.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: Brute force: O(n squared) time, O(1) space. Optimized: O(n) time, O(n) space. Further optimized (two pointers): O(n) time, O(1) space.

items: Pattern: precomputed left and right maximum arrays, further reduced to two pointers converging inward using a running max on each side.

Core Idea: water at a position is bounded by the shorter of its two surrounding walls, and whichever side currently has the smaller running max always has its water level already fully determined, letting two pointers replace two full precomputed arrays.
Time: O(n squared) for the brute force, O(n) for both optimized versions.
Space: O(1) for the brute force, O(n) for the precomputed array version, O(1) for the two pointer version.
Most Important Observation: the taller of the two surrounding walls never needs to be known exactly, only that it is at least as tall as the smaller side's running max.
Interview Difficulty: the precomputed array version is straightforward; correctly proving and applying the two pointer invariant is what shows real algorithmic depth.
One line memory trick: always process the side with the smaller wall, since its water level is already settled.
